facts.fact_text: On 10 December 2010 eight individuals, none of whom are applicants in the present case, submitted notice of a public demonstration to the mayor of Moscow.
The notice indicated that a meeting would be held from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m. on Triumfalnaya Square, Moscow.
The organisers estimated that about 1,500 people would take part in the event at Triumfalnaya Square on 31 December 2010.

The notice stated that the proposed demonstration was intended to demand respect for the constitutional right to peaceful demonstration and assembly guaranteed by Article 31 of the Constitution of the Russian Federation.
The organisers indicated that it would not be necessary to divert the traffic for the proposed demonstration.
On 22 December 2010 the Moscow Government's Department for Liaison with Security Authorities informed the organisers that the event had been approved by the deputy mayor of Moscow.
The number of participants in the approved demonstration at Triumfalnaya Square was limited to 1,000.
The authorised meeting began at 6 p.m. on 31 December 2010 at Triumfalnaya Square, as planned.
The applicant claimed that he had arrived at the meeting at Triumfalnaya Square with his daughter.
The applicant claimed that he had parked his car at Tverskaya Street.

During the meeting at Triumfalnaya Square on 31 December 2010, the applicant addressed the participants with a speech in which he criticised the criminal conviction of Mikhail Khodorkovskiy, the former owner of the Yukos oil company.

During the meeting at Triumfalnaya Square on 31 December 2010, the applicant addressed the participants with a speech in which he criticised the criminal conviction of Platon Lebedev, associate of Mikhail Khodorkovskiy.
During the meeting at Triumfalnaya Square on 31 December 2010, the applicant condemned the corruption in the State administration.
During the meeting at Triumfalnaya Square on 31 December 2010, the applicant chanted the slogan "The authorities to resign!".
During the meeting at Triumfalnaya Square on 31 December 2010, the applicant chanted the slogan "Putin to resign!".
During the meeting at Triumfalnaya Square on 31 December 2010, the applicant chanted the slogan "Happy New Year without Putin!".
According to the applicant, the perimeter of Triumfalnaya Square was cordoned off and guarded by the riot police on 31 December 2010.
The applicant claimed that he and his daughter had entered Triumfalnaya Square from Tverskaya Street through the only opening in the cordon.
At the end of the meeting at Triumfalnaya Square on 31 December 2010, the applicant, accompanied by his daughter, headed across Triumfalnaya Square towards Tverskaya Street.
At the exit from Triumfalnaya Square, the applicant saw the riot police arresting one of the participants in the demonstration.
Shortly after seeing the riot police arrest a participant, the applicant was also arrested and put into a police vehicle.
The applicant claimed that on the way to his car his passage had been obstructed by police officers.
The applicant claimed that he heard a police instruction over a loudspeaker calling for people to stay calm and to pass through.
The applicant claimed that he was arrested without any warning or explanation.
The applicant claimed that he had not disobeyed or resisted the police and had followed their instructions to pass through.
The Government alleged that two police officers, Sergeant X and Private Y, had warned the applicant and ordered him to stop agitating the crowd and to return to the authorised meeting.
The Government contended that the applicant had ignored the warning from Sergeant X and Private Y and had continued shouting out slogans and disobeying the police.
The Government contended that Sergeant X and Private Y arrested the applicant after he ignored their warning and continued shouting slogans and disobeying the police.
At 7 p.m. on 31 December 2010 the applicant was taken to the police station of the Tverskoy District Department of the Interior.

At 7.10 p.m. on 31 December 2010, Private Y drew up a report stating that the applicant had been escorted to the Tverskoy District Department of the Interior police station in order to draw up the administrative material.

At 7.10 p.m. on 31 December 2010, the on-duty police officer at the Tverskoy District Department of the Interior drew up a report on the applicant's administrative arrest under Article 27.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences, stating that the applicant had been arrested in order to draw up the administrative material.

Both Sergeant X and Private Y produced identical duty reports stating that on 31 December 2010 at 18.30 Boris Yefimovich Nemtsov was apprehended because he had disobeyed a lawful order of the police in connection with Sergeant X and Private Y performing their duty of maintaining public order and safeguarding the public.

The duty reports of Sergeant X and Private Y stated that the applicant stood at 31 Tverskaya Street and began to shout "Down with Putin!", "Russia without Putin!" as well as insults to President Medvedev, catching people's attention and calling them to come to the Mayakovskiy monument for a meeting.
The applicant alleged that being obliged to stand throughout the trial had further aggravated his fatigue and hampered the conduct of his defence.
The applicant claimed at the hearing that he had been detained for no reason other than political oppression.
The applicant contested the content of the police reports, in particular the statement that the police had given him a warning or an order which he could have disobeyed.
At the applicant's request, the Justice of the Peace called and examined thirteen witnesses who had been at the scene of the authorised demonstration at Triumfalnaya Square on 31 December 2010.

The thirteen witnesses testified that they had heard the applicant addressing the meeting at Triumfalnaya Square and that after his speech he had said farewell and left; he had not made any calls to go on to another meeting.
Six of the thirteen witnesses testified that they had left the meeting at the same time as the applicant and had witnessed his arrest.

Six witnesses testified that the exit from the meeting at Triumfalnaya Square had been blocked by the riot police and the crowd had begun to build up because those who wanted to leave could not do so.
Six witnesses testified that when the applicant arrived at the cordon the police surrounded him so as to separate him from others wanting to leave the meeting, and arrested him.
Eight witnesses stated that the applicant had not been shouting any slogans and had not been acting against the police orders before being surrounded and arrested.
Witness M.T. stated that she had heard the applicant asking the riot police why the exit had been blocked.

Witness M.T. stated that she had heard the applicant shouting that Article 31 of the Constitution of the Russian Federation guaranteed the freedom of assembly, but he had not shouted any calls or obscenities.
The remaining witnesses at the hearing before the Justice of the Peace had not seen the actual arrest of the applicant.
The applicant's daughter and her friend testified that they had been walking back to the car with the applicant and talking about the plans for New Year's eve when they arrived at the police cordon.

The applicant's daughter and her friend testified that they had lost sight of the applicant in the crowd at the police cordon, and one or two minutes later had called him on his mobile phone and found out that he had been arrested.
The Justice of the Peace called and examined two policemen, Sergeant X and Private Y, who had signed the reports stating that they had arrested the applicant because he had disobeyed their orders.
Sergeant X and Private Y testified that on 31 December 2010 they had been on duty maintaining public order at Triumfalnaya Square.
Sergeant X and Private Y testified that they had seen the applicant at 31 Tverskaya Street shouting anti-government slogans and calling people around him to hold an unauthorised meeting.

Sergeant X and Private Y testified that they had approached the applicant and requested him to stop agitating outside the authorised meeting and to return to the place allocated for the meeting to speak there.
Sergeant X and Private Y testified that the applicant had not reacted to their requests, so they had asked him to proceed to the police van.
Sergeant X and Private Y testified that the applicant had disobeyed the order to proceed to the police van and had been arrested; he had put up resistance while being arrested.
On 2 January 2011 the Justice of the Peace found that the applicant had disobeyed the police orders to stop chanting anti-government slogans and had resisted lawful arrest.

The Justice of the Peace based her findings on the witness statements of Sergeant X and Private Y, their written reports of 31 December 2010, their written statements of the same date, the report on the administrative arrest of the same date, the notice of the public demonstration of 16 December 2010, and the reply of 22 December 2010 indicating that the second demonstration had not been authorised.
The Justice of the Peace dismissed the applicant's testimony on the grounds that as a defendant, he would have sought to exonerate himself from administrative liability.

The Justice of the Peace dismissed the testimonies of seven eyewitnesses on the grounds that they had contradicted the policemen's testimonies and because those witnesses had been acquainted with the applicant, had taken part in the same demonstration and therefore must have been biased towards the applicant.
The testimonies of the remaining six witnesses were dismissed by the Justice of the Peace as irrelevant.
The applicant was found guilty of having disobeyed a lawful order of the police, in breach of Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The applicant was sentenced to fifteen days' administrative detention.

Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that failure to obey a lawful order or demand of a police officer in connection with the performance of their official duties related to maintaining public order and security, or impeding the performance by them of their official duties, shall be punishable by a fine of between five hundred and one thousand roubles or by administrative detention of up to fifteen days.

Article 27.2 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the escorting or transfer by force of an individual for the purpose of drawing up an administrative offence report, if this cannot be done at the place where the offence was discovered and if the drawing up of a report is mandatory, shall be carried out by the police.
Article 27.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the escort operation shall be carried out as quickly as possible.

Article 27.2 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the escort operation shall be recorded in an escort operation report, an administrative offence report or an administrative detention report, and the escorted person shall be given a copy of the escort operation report if he or she so requests.

Article 27.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that administrative detention or short-term restriction of an individual's liberty may be applied in exceptional cases if this is necessary for the prompt and proper examination of the alleged administrative offence or to secure the enforcement of any penalty imposed by a judgment concerning an administrative offence.

Article 27.3 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that where the detained person so requests, his family, the administrative department at his place of work or study and his defence counsel shall be informed of his whereabouts.

Article 27.3 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the detained person shall have his rights and obligations under the Code explained to him, and the corresponding entry shall be made in the administrative arrest report.
Article 27.4 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that administrative detention shall be recorded in a report.
Article 27.4 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that if he or she so requests, the detained person shall be given a copy of the administrative detention report.

Article 27.5 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the duration of administrative detention shall not exceed three hours, except in the cases set out in paragraphs 2 and 3 of that Article.

Article 27.5 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that persons subject to administrative proceedings concerning offences involving unlawful crossing of the Russian border may be subject to administrative detention for up to 48 hours.

Article 27.5 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that persons subject to administrative proceedings concerning offences punishable, among other administrative sanctions, by administrative detention may be subject to administrative detention for up to 48 hours.

At the hearing before the Justice of the Peace on 2 January 2011, the applicant requested that the recording made by Mr T., an independent photographer, be admitted as evidence.

At the hearing before the Justice of the Peace on 2 January 2011, the applicant requested that the court obtain from the prosecution the video recording made by the Moscow police at the scene of the public demonstration.

At the hearing before the Justice of the Peace on 2 January 2011, the applicant requested that the court call and cross-examine Police Colonel B. about the circumstances of the applicant's arrest, which Police Colonel B. had commented on in the media.
The Justice of the Peace dismissed the applicant's request to admit the video recordings on the grounds that the provenance of the recordings was not supported by evidence.

The Justice of the Peace refused to order that the video recording made by the police be admitted as evidence, stating that the applicant's request was not specific enough and that the applicant had failed to prove the existence of any such recordings.
The Justice of the Peace refused to call and examine Police Colonel B. as a witness, having considered that request irrelevant.

In his appeal the applicant claimed that his arrest and conviction for the administrative offence had been in breach of domestic law and in violation of the Convention.
In his appeal the applicant alleged that his right to freedom of expression had been violated.
In his appeal the applicant alleged that his right to freedom of assembly had been violated.
In his appeal the applicant contested the findings of fact made by the Justice of the Peace as regards his conduct after he had left the meeting at Triumfalnaya Square.
In his appeal the applicant challenged the Justice of the Peace's refusal to admit the photographic and video materials as evidence or to obtain the footage of the demonstration shot by the police.

In his appeal the applicant complained about the manner in which the first-instance hearing had been conducted, in particular alleging that the Justice of the Peace had ordered him to stand throughout the hearing, which had been humiliating and had made it difficult to participate in the proceedings.
In his appeal the applicant complained about the conditions of his detention at the Tverskoy District Department of the Interior police station from 31 December 2010 to 2 January 2011.
On 12 January 2011 the Tverskoy District Court examined the applicant's appeal against the judgment of the Justice of the Peace.
At the applicant's request, the Tverskoy District Court kept verbatim records of the appeal hearing on 12 January 2011.

During the appeal hearing on 12 January 2011, the applicant complained of the alleged unlawfulness of his arrest and the poor conditions of his detention at the Tverskoy District Department of the Interior police station.

During the appeal hearing on 12 January 2011, the applicant asked the Tverskoy District Court to declare the acts of the police who had detained him for over forty hours before bringing him before a court unlawful.
At the appeal hearing on 12 January 2011, the applicant reiterated his requests that the court admit three video recordings of his arrest as evidence.
At the appeal hearing on 12 January 2011, the applicant reiterated his request that the court obtain the video recording made by the Moscow police at the scene of the public demonstration.
At the appeal hearing on 12 January 2011, the applicant requested that two photographs of his arrest be admitted as evidence.
At the appeal hearing on 12 January 2011, the applicant asked the court to call and examine photographer T. as a witness.
At the appeal hearing on 12 January 2011, the applicant asked the court to cross-examine police officers Sergeant X and Private Y again.
The Tverskoy District Court granted the request to admit one video recording as evidence at the appeal hearing on 12 January 2011.
The Tverskoy District Court granted the request to admit two photographs as evidence at the appeal hearing on 12 January 2011.
The Tverskoy District Court decided to call and examine photographer T. as a witness at the appeal hearing on 12 January 2011.

The Tverskoy District Court rejected all other requests made by the applicant at the appeal hearing on 12 January 2011, including the request to obtain the police video recording and to cross-examine Sergeant X and Private Y again.

Photographer T. testified at the appeal hearing that he had gone to the meeting at Triumfalnaya Square to film it and had been waiting for the applicant at the exit because he had wanted to interview him.

Photographer T. testified that when the applicant approached the exit from Triumfalnaya Square, a big group of policemen rushed over to block his way and there had been a minute's pause when a crowd began to build up against the cordon, blocking the passage.
Photographer T. testified that one person was arrested, and about thirty seconds later someone else, and then the applicant.

Photographer T. testified that he saw the applicant's arrest while filming it from a distance of about five or six metres, separated from the applicant by several rows of people, of which two rows consisted of policemen.
Photographer T. testified that his recording began a few minutes before the arrest and continued without any interruption until the applicant had been put in the police van.
Photographer T. testified that the applicant had not put up any resistance to the officers arresting him.

Photographer T. identified on a photograph the officer wearing a fur hat who had arrested the applicant, and explained that that person had taken the applicant out of the crowd and then passed him on to another policeman in order to put the applicant into the police van.
Photographer T. testified that the applicant had not shouted any slogans or insults and had repeated "Easy, easy" to the policemen while being escorted to the van.
Photographer T. testified that the applicant had been standing throughout the first-instance hearing before the Justice of the Peace, while his counsel had been sitting on a chair.
The Tverskoy District Court watched the video recording made by photographer T. at the appeal hearing on 12 January 2011.
The Tverskoy District Court decided not to take cognisance of photographer T.'s testimonies, his recording or the photograph submitted at the appeal hearing.

The Tverskoy District Court found that the footage showed a large number of people gathered at 31 Tverskaya Street in Moscow, with the applicant at the centre, and that a policeman addressed the citizens through a loudspeaker with a request to disperse and not to block the passage, but the applicant remained standing in one place addressing the gathered citizens.

The Tverskoy District Court found that the video operator was at such a distance from the applicant that he was separated from him by several rows of people, including gathered citizens and riot police, making it impossible to understand what the citizens and the applicant were saying.

The Tverskoy District Court found that the recording of the applicant was interrupted as the camera pointed away onto the policemen putting the first arrested person, and then another one, into the police vans, and only afterwards showed the applicant being led to a police van by policemen without putting up resistance.

The Tverskoy District Court concluded that the submitted footage did not show the applicant's actions immediately before his placement in the police van and did not depict the applicant addressing the citizens before he was detained, and therefore did not refute the testimonies of Sergeant X and Private Y.

The Tverskoy District Court found that photographer T.'s testimony could not refute the testimonies of Sergeant X and Private Y because T. had observed only those actions of the applicant that appeared on the footage.

The Tverskoy District Court found that the photographs submitted during the appeal hearing depicting the applicant surrounded by policemen, one of whom was supporting his arm, could not be considered as refuting the event of the offence or the evidence, including the testimonies of Sergeant X and Private Y, because of the absence of information on the exact time of their taking or their connection with the place.
On 12 January 2011 the Tverskoy District Court dismissed the applicant's appeal and upheld the first-instance judgment of the Justice of the Peace.
The Tverskoy District Court found, on the basis of the testimonies and reports of Sergeant X and Private Y, that the applicant had indeed been guilty of having disobeyed a lawful order of the police.
The Tverskoy District Court upheld the reasoning of the Justice of the Peace whereby it rejected the testimonies of thirteen witnesses called at the applicant's request.
The Tverskoy District Court found no reason to mistrust the testimonies of Sergeant X and Private Y because they had had no personal interest in the outcome of the applicant's case.

In its appeal decision of 12 January 2011, the Tverskoy District Court addressed the lawfulness of the applicant's detention pending the first-instance trial and considered that there had been no breach.

The Tverskoy District Court's appeal decision stated that after the report on the administrative offence had been drawn up, the information necessary for establishing the circumstances of the committed offence was collected, including the explanations of Sergeant X and Private Y, the notice of the place of the public demonstration of 31 December 2010, the mayor's reply to that notice, and the personal characteristics of the applicant.

The Tverskoy District Court's appeal decision referred to a ruling made by the Justice of the Peace of 2 September 2010 convicting the applicant of an offence under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The Tverskoy District Court's appeal decision held that the applicant's detention during less than 48 hours was not in breach of Article 27.5 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The Tverskoy District Court found that the applicant's complaints about the conditions of his detention between 31 December 2010 and 2 January 2011 were outside the scope of the appeal proceedings, holding that another type of legal action should have been brought by the applicant to challenge those acts.
The Tverskoy District Court did not specify what procedure the applicant should have followed as an avenue for his complaints about the conditions of detention.

On 31 March 2011 the applicant lodged before the Tverskoy District Court a complaint under Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, challenging his initial arrest and complaining of the poor conditions of detention for over forty hours.

On 4 April 2011 the Tverskoy District Court refused to accept the applicant's action under Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, holding that the questions concerning the lawfulness of the police acts had to be examined in the relevant administrative proceedings and could not be dealt with in civil proceedings.
On 14 April 2011 the applicant appealed against the Tverskoy District Court's refusal to accept his complaint under Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The Moscow City Court dismissed the applicant's appeal on 22 July 2011.
The Moscow City Court relied on Ruling no. 2 of 10 February 2009 by the Plenary Supreme Court of the Russian Federation in dismissing the applicant's appeal.

The Moscow City Court held that courts may not examine complaints lodged under Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure against acts or inaction connected with the application of the Code of Administrative Offences, Chapter 30 of which provides for the procedure for challenging them.

The Moscow City Court held that acts or inaction inseparable from an administrative case may not be subject to a separate challenge, and that arguments against the admissibility of evidence or the application of a precautionary measure may be put forward during the hearing of the administrative case or in points of appeal against the judgment.

The Moscow City Court held that if administrative proceedings are terminated, acts committed in the course of those proceedings that entailed a breach of an individual's rights or freedoms, or hindered the exercise of their rights and freedoms, or imposed an obligation after the proceedings had been terminated, may be challenged under Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The Moscow City Court held that acts of officials where no administrative file has been opened may be challenged under Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The applicant attempted to challenge the acts of the judiciary involved in his case before the Judiciary Qualification Board of Moscow.
The applicant's attempts to challenge the acts of the judiciary before the Judiciary Qualification Board of Moscow were unsuccessful.
